course.title: SecAI+ Capstone: Four Releases
course.audience: Secure an AI product end to end: attack it, defend it, watch it, govern it, release it.
course.description: Secure the AI at the center of a facility-services company. Every week ships a complete release: attack cases with evidence, controls, monitoring, governance and a signed release note.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).

glossary.data.src_ip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a network (Suricata) alert — who the traffic came from.
glossary.data.srcip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a host alert (logins, web requests). Its network twin is data.src_ip — search both.
glossary.ossec.conf: The Wazuh agent's config file. It names the SOC to report to and any extra log files to ship.
glossary.hydra: A password-guessing tool. In this lab you run it against your own pod so the SOC has a brute-force attack to detect.
glossary.tcpdump: A command-line tool that records network traffic to a .pcap file you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.Wireshark: A traffic viewer. Open a .pcap in it and "Follow HTTP Stream" to read the exact request an attacker sent.
glossary.Kali: The attacker machine in your lab — a Linux build that ships with nmap, nikto, hydra and the rest.
glossary.Proxmox: A hypervisor — an operating system whose job is to run virtual machines. In Server+ you install it on your own server; in the CySA lab it already runs the lab.
glossary.POST: Power-On Self-Test — the hardware check a machine runs the moment you power it on, before any operating system. Beeps and blink codes are POST talking to you.
glossary.DIMM: A memory stick. Which slots they go in is dictated by the motherboard manual, and the wrong slots can stop the machine starting at all.
glossary.ECC: Error-Correcting Code memory — server RAM that detects and fixes single-bit corruption on the fly. Servers use it; desktops usually do not.
glossary.HCL: Hardware Compatibility List — the check that the software you plan to run officially supports the exact hardware you have, before you build on it.
glossary.UEFI: The modern replacement for the old BIOS firmware. Boot mode matters: an OS installed under UEFI will not boot if the firmware is later switched to legacy.
glossary.IOMMU: The chip feature (Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi) that lets a virtual machine be handed a real piece of hardware, like a NIC, as its own.
glossary.VT-x: Intel’s virtualization extensions. Present is not enough — they must be ENABLED in firmware setup, or the hypervisor cannot start a single VM.
glossary.stripe size: How large a chunk of data a RAID array writes to one disk before moving to the next. The default is right for this build.
glossary.IDS: Intrusion Detection System — software that watches traffic and raises an alert when it matches a known attack pattern. Suricata is yours.
glossary.NVD: National Vulnerability Database — the public catalogue you search to find a CVE and its score for a given software version.
glossary.pod: Your team’s pair of machines: one Ubuntu web server and one Windows PC.
glossary.escalate: Pass an alert on for deeper investigation, with the reason written down, instead of closing it yourself.
glossary.SOC: Security Operations Centre — the team (and dashboard) that watches for attacks around the clock.
glossary.SIEM: Security Information and Event Management — software that gathers logs from everywhere and raises alerts. Wazuh is your SIEM.
glossary.IOC: Indicator of Compromise — a clue an attacker leaves behind, like a bad IP address, file name, or hash.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public ID for one specific known software flaw, e.g. CVE-2021-41773.
glossary.CVSS: A 0–10 score for how severe a vulnerability is, so you can rank what to fix first.
glossary.pcap: A 'packet capture' — a saved recording of network traffic you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.SQLi: SQL injection — tricking a website into running database commands it shouldn't, often to steal data.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall — a filter in front of a website that blocks common attacks like SQL injection.
glossary.POA&M: Plan of Action & Milestones — a to-do list for fixing findings: what, who owns it, and by when.
glossary.PTES: Penetration Testing Execution Standard — the agreed steps of a pentest: recon, scan, exploit, report.
glossary.STRIDE: A checklist of threat types: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
glossary.NIC: Network Interface Card — a machine's network connection. On these VMs it's usually named ens18.
glossary.IaC: Infrastructure as Code — describing machines in a text file a tool applies, so the build is repeatable and the file is the record. Terraform or OpenTofu is yours.
glossary.OpenTofu: The open-source fork of Terraform, kept under the Linux Foundation after HashiCorp changed Terraform’s licence in 2023. Same HCL, same providers, same state files; the command is tofu instead of terraform.
glossary.exporter: A small program on a host that publishes its metrics on an HTTP port for Prometheus to collect. node_exporter for Linux, windows_exporter for Windows.
glossary.IPAM: IP Address Management — the tool that holds every subnet and address and who has it, so the plan and reality are the same document. NetBox is yours.
glossary.FIM: File Integrity Monitoring — an agent that hashes important files and alerts when one changes, which is how a tampered config gets noticed.
glossary.cloud-init: The first-boot setup a cloud image runs: hostname, user, keys and addressing handed in from outside, so a clone comes up configured instead of blank.
glossary.DNAT: Destination NAT — the host rewriting where a packet is going. The rule that turns a request to the host’s campus address on port 80 into a request to websrv in the DMZ.
glossary.MASQUERADE: Source NAT behind the host’s own address, so a reply from the campus LAN or the internet comes back to the host and is handed to the guest that asked.
glossary.published port: A port on the host’s campus address that a DNAT rule hands to a VM behind it. Each one is a deliberate hole in the segmentation, and you should be able to say why it exists.
glossary.idempotent: Running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The property that makes a playbook safe to run every night — and why changed=0 on the second run is the proof.
glossary.drift: Reality diverging from what the code says — a change made in the console instead of the repository. terraform plan (tofu plan) detects it; the next apply may undo it.
glossary.dynamic inventory: Ansible asking the hypervisor which hosts exist instead of reading a list someone typed. The list is never out of date because there is no list.
glossary.XDR: Extended Detection and Response — one platform watching endpoints, logs and files across a whole fleet. Wazuh on the Core is the MSP’s.
glossary.verify job: The backup server re-reading a backup, chunk by chunk, to confirm it is restorable before anyone needs it.
glossary.SLO: Service Level Objective — the availability you promise a client, as a number. The SLA is the contract around it.
glossary.SCA: Security Configuration Assessment — checking a machine's settings against a hardening benchmark.
glossary.Rules of Engagement: The written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.RoE: Rules of Engagement — the written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.triage: Quickly sorting alerts into real vs noise and deciding what to escalate — like an ER nurse.
glossary.baseline: A record of what 'normal' looks like, so you can spot what's abnormal later.
glossary.chain of custody: A documented trail of who handled each piece of evidence and when — so it holds up as proof.
glossary.agent: A small program installed on each machine that ships its logs to the SOC.
glossary.gate: A checkpoint at the end of a week — finish its required work before the next week unlocks.
glossary.eve.json: The file where Suricata writes its network alerts.
glossary.subnet: A slice of a network sharing an address range, e.g. 10.10.100.x.
glossary.Wazuh: The free, open-source SIEM/SOC platform this lab is built on.
glossary.Suricata: An open-source network intrusion detector that watches traffic and raises alerts.
glossary.Sysmon: A Windows tool that records detailed activity — processes, connections, file changes.
glossary.DVWA: Damn Vulnerable Web App — a deliberately insecure web app used as a safe attack target.
glossary.nmap: A scanner that finds open ports and what software is running on them.
glossary.nikto: A scanner that checks a web server for known issues.
glossary.MITRE ATT&CK: A public catalogue of attacker techniques, used to describe how an attack was carried out.
glossary.MTTD: Mean Time To Detect — the average time from an attack starting to it being noticed.
glossary.MTTR: Mean Time To Respond — the average time from detecting an attack to containing it.
glossary.rule.level: Wazuh scores every alert 0–15 by severity; searching rule.level:>=7 keeps the ones that usually matter.
glossary.rule.groups: The category tags Wazuh puts on an alert (e.g. authentication_failed, ids, web) — handy for filtering by attack type.
glossary.agent.name: The Wazuh field naming which machine an alert came from (e.g. Team07-ubuntu) — use it to filter to one host.
glossary.event channel: A named Windows log stream — Sysmon writes to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational, which the agent forwards.
glossary.Emerging Threats ruleset: The community alert rules Suricata downloads with suricata-update — without them it sees traffic but raises nothing.
glossary.DQL: Dashboard Query Language — the field:value search syntax in the Wazuh/OpenSearch search bar (e.g. data.src_ip:10.10.30.7).
glossary.Discover: The Wazuh/OpenSearch view that lists raw events in a table you can search, add columns to, and save.
glossary.time picker: The date/time control (top-right) that sets which window of events you see — the #1 reason a correct search looks empty.
glossary.visualization: A saved chart (bar, pie, table) built from a search — the building block you drop onto a dashboard.
glossary.dashboard: A saved page of visualizations and searches you assemble to watch at a glance.
glossary.rule.description: The Wazuh field holding the human-readable name of the rule that fired — useful to group and count alerts by.
glossary.syscheck: Wazuh’s File Integrity Monitoring engine; its events carry syscheck.path and whether a file was added/modified/deleted.
glossary.sensor: A program on a machine that watches activity and reports it to the SOC — your Wazuh agent, Suricata and Sysmon are all sensors.
glossary.endpoint: Any individual computer on the network — a laptop, server or VM — as opposed to the network gear between them.
glossary.telemetry: The stream of activity data a machine sends about itself — processes, logins, connections — that the SOC watches.
glossary.hash: A short fingerprint calculated from a file; change one byte and the fingerprint changes, so it proves the file was not tampered with.
glossary.hashing: Running a file through a formula to get its fixed-length fingerprint (its hash).
glossary.SHA-256: A widely trusted hashing method that turns any file into a 64-character fingerprint.
glossary.false positive: An alert that turned out to be harmless — the tool flagged something that was not actually an attack.
glossary.true positive: An alert that was real — the flagged activity really was malicious.
glossary.enroll: To register a machine with the SOC so its agent starts sending logs.
glossary.brute force: Guessing a password by automatically trying huge numbers of combinations until one works.
glossary.port scan: Probing a machine to list which network ports are open, to discover what services it is running.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell — a way to log in to and run commands on another machine over the network, from your terminal.
glossary.pivot: To follow a clue (like an IP or username) from one log into related events, tracing an attacker’s movements.
glossary.hardening: Making a machine harder to attack by closing unused services, fixing weak settings and applying updates.
glossary.containment: Stopping an attack from spreading — e.g. isolating the affected machine — once you have detected it.
glossary.vulnerability: A weakness in software or configuration that an attacker could exploit.
glossary.vuln: Short for vulnerability — a weakness an attacker could exploit.
glossary.firewall: A filter that allows or blocks network connections by rule, to keep unwanted traffic out.
glossary.ufw: Uncomplicated Firewall — the simple command-line firewall on Ubuntu (e.g. ufw allow 22).
glossary.VLAN: A virtual LAN — one physical switch split into separate networks. Ports in different VLANs cannot talk without something routing between them, which is the whole point.
glossary.trunk: A link between switches that carries several VLANs at once, tagging each frame with its VLAN id (802.1Q). The alternative is one cable per VLAN.
glossary.native VLAN: The one VLAN a trunk carries UNTAGGED. If the two ends disagree about which it is, traffic silently lands in the wrong network — the classic trunk fault.
glossary.SVI: Switched Virtual Interface — a VLAN’s gateway configured on the switch itself. A switch with SVIs routes between VLANs at wire speed; a switch without them needs a router.
glossary.router-on-a-stick: Inter-VLAN routing done by a router over a single trunk, with one subinterface per VLAN. What you build when the switch cannot route — same outcome, one link carrying all of it.
glossary.EtherChannel: Two or more physical links bundled into one logical link, so a cable can fail without an outage and the bandwidth adds up. LACP is the protocol that negotiates it.
glossary.spanning tree: The protocol that stops a loop when switches have more than one path between them, by blocking all but one. It always picks a root switch — set it deliberately or it picks the oldest one.
glossary.PortFast: Tells spanning tree an access port has a PC on it, not a switch, so it forwards immediately instead of waiting. Never on a port that could reach another switch.
glossary.BPDU Guard: Shuts a PortFast port the moment it hears spanning-tree messages — which means somebody plugged a switch into a desk port. The protection that makes PortFast safe.
glossary.OSPF: A routing protocol: routers tell each other which networks they can reach, so each works out its own routes. It replaces static routes and reacts when a link dies.
glossary.OSPF area: A grouping that limits how far routing detail spreads. This course uses a single area 0 — the backbone — because one correctly adjacent area is the CCNA outcome.
glossary.adjacency: Two OSPF routers that have agreed to exchange routes. It has to reach the FULL state; anything less is the protocol telling you what does not match.
glossary.NAT: Network Address Translation — rewriting addresses as traffic crosses the edge, so internal addresses that mean nothing on the internet can still reach it.
glossary.PAT: Port Address Translation, sometimes "NAT overload" — the whole company sharing one public address, told apart by port number. What almost every small site actually runs.
glossary.ACL: Access Control List — an ordered list of permit and deny rules applied to an interface in one direction. It ends with an implicit deny, which is why the order matters.
glossary.port security: Limits which or how many MAC addresses a switch port accepts, so a stranger plugging into a desk port cannot quietly join the network.
glossary.ip helper-address: Tells a router to forward DHCP requests from a VLAN to a DHCP server somewhere else. The enterprise pattern, versus the router serving DHCP itself.
glossary.SNMP: The protocol a monitoring system uses to read a device’s interfaces, CPU and memory. Read-only is all a NOC needs; v3 is the version with real authentication.
glossary.syslog: Device log messages sent to a central collector. With synchronised clocks it turns "it broke this morning" into a readable sequence across every device.
glossary.NetBox: The source of truth for the network: sites, devices, interfaces, cables, VLANs and prefixes, with an API. It replaces the spreadsheet once the spreadsheet stops scaling.
glossary.Oxidized: Collects every device’s configuration on a schedule and commits it to Git, so you have both a backup and a history of what changed.
glossary.source of truth: The one system that DEFINES what the network should be. Tools read from it and configure devices to match, so the documentation cannot drift from reality.
glossary.PoE: Power over Ethernet — the switch powering the device on the far end of the cable, which is how phones and access points run without a plug of their own.
glossary.SFP: The slot a fibre (or copper) transceiver plugs into, for uplinks that go further or faster than the built-in ports.
glossary.resource group: Azure’s folder for resources. Everything in it shares a lifecycle: delete the group and everything inside goes with it.
glossary.VNet: Virtual network — your own private network inside Azure, with an address range you choose. AWS calls it a VPC.
glossary.VPC: Virtual Private Cloud — your own private network inside AWS, with an address range you choose. Azure calls it a VNet.
glossary.NSG: Network security group — Azure’s firewall rule set for a subnet or a network card. Rules are checked by priority, lowest number first.
glossary.security group: AWS’s firewall around an instance. It only has allow rules: anything not allowed is blocked, and replies to allowed traffic are let back in automatically.
glossary.CIDR: The slash notation for an address range: 10.10.0.0/16 means the first 16 bits are fixed, leaving 65,536 addresses. /24 leaves 256.
glossary.RFC 1918: The three private address ranges (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x) that never route on the public internet, so every company can reuse them.
glossary.RBAC: Role-based access control — Azure’s way of granting access: a person or group gets a role (Reader, Contributor, Owner) at a scope (subscription, group, resource).
glossary.IAM: Identity and Access Management — AWS’s service for users, groups, roles and the policies that say what each may do.
glossary.managed identity: An identity Azure gives a resource (like a Function) so it can sign in to other services with no password or key stored anywhere.
glossary.IAM role: An identity a service (like a Lambda function or an EC2 instance) assumes to get short-lived credentials — the AWS equivalent of a managed identity.
glossary.tags: Key=value labels on a resource (owner=team01-infra). They carry what a name cannot: who to ask, which environment, which cost centre.
glossary.$5 budget: A spending limit with alerts. It does not stop spending by itself — it emails you before a mistake becomes expensive.
glossary.TLS 1.2: The minimum modern version of the encryption behind HTTPS. Older versions have known weaknesses, so servers are told to refuse them.
glossary.SSH key: A key pair for signing in to a Linux machine: the public half goes on the server, the private half stays with you. No password exists to guess.
glossary.key pair: AWS’s name for an SSH key pair. The private .pem file is shown once at creation — download it and keep it out of the repository.
glossary.deallocate: Stop an Azure VM so its compute is released and stops billing. A shutdown from inside the OS leaves it “stopped” but still allocated and still paid for.
glossary.public IP: An internet-routable address on a resource. It is what the outside world (and your SSH test) reaches; the private IP is what other resources use.
glossary.IMDSv2: The token-based version of the instance metadata service on EC2. Requiring it blocks a common trick that steals an instance’s credentials.
glossary.static website: A site made of plain files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) served straight from storage — no web server to run or patch.
glossary.S3: Simple Storage Service — AWS object storage. A bucket holds files; the name is unique across all of AWS.
glossary.CloudFront: AWS’s content delivery network. It sits in front of the bucket, serves the site over HTTPS, and caches copies near visitors.
glossary.OAC: Origin Access Control — the setting that lets CloudFront read a private bucket on your behalf, so the bucket itself never becomes public.
glossary.serverless: Code or a database you pay for per request, with no server to size, patch or switch off. Idle means free.
glossary.Consumption plan: The Azure Functions plan that bills per execution and scales to zero. The first million executions a month are free.
glossary.Lambda: AWS’s serverless code service: upload a function, it runs when triggered, and you pay per call.
glossary.API Gateway: The AWS front door for an API: it gives your function an HTTPS URL and handles CORS.
glossary.Cosmos DB: Azure’s globally distributed NoSQL database. In serverless mode it bills per request unit used.
glossary.DynamoDB: AWS’s NoSQL key-value database. On-demand mode bills per request; 25 GB is always free.
glossary.partition key: The field a NoSQL database uses to decide where an item is stored. Chosen at creation, and cannot be changed later.
glossary.binding: An Azure Functions shortcut that connects a function to a service (like Cosmos DB) through configuration, so the code never opens a connection itself.
glossary.CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — the browser rule that lets a page from one site read an API’s answer only if the API lists that site as an allowed origin.
glossary.allowed origin: The scheme, host and port of a page (https://mysite.example). CORS decides per origin which pages may read an API.
glossary.Application Insights: Azure’s application monitoring: every request, failure and exception from the Function, searchable.
glossary.CloudWatch: AWS’s monitoring service: logs, metrics and alarms in one place.
glossary.action group: Azure’s “who gets told and how” list. Alerts point at it, so the email address changes in one place.
glossary.SNS: Simple Notification Service — AWS’s “who gets told” topic. Alarms publish to it; email subscribers must confirm once.
glossary.Key Vault: Azure’s safe for secrets, keys and certificates. An app setting can point at a secret instead of holding it.
glossary.Cost Explorer: AWS’s cost report. Must be enabled once and takes up to a day to fill; the console view is free, the API is not.
glossary.Free Tier: What AWS gives away: some things for 12 months after the account opens (750 EC2 hours a month), some always (Lambda, DynamoDB).
glossary.Cloud Shell: A terminal in the browser with the Azure CLI signed in already. It needs a small storage share the first time.
glossary.CloudShell: A terminal in the browser with the AWS CLI signed in already. Free.
glossary.shared responsibility: Who secures what: the provider runs the datacenter, hardware and (for PaaS) the platform; you own your data, identities, configuration and — on a VM — the operating system.
glossary.IaaS: Infrastructure as a Service — you rent a machine and network and manage the operating system yourself. A VM is IaaS.
glossary.PaaS: Platform as a Service — you bring code and data; the provider runs and patches the platform. Functions, a static website and a managed database are PaaS.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service — a finished application you sign in to, like Microsoft 365 or the GitHub website.
glossary.availability zone: One of several separate datacenters inside a region, with its own power and cooling. Two zones fail independently; one region can still fail as a whole.
glossary.resource lock: An Azure setting on a resource or group that refuses deletes (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly) until someone removes the lock first.
glossary.Advisor: Azure’s free recommendation service: cost, security, reliability, performance and operational tips for what you have deployed.
glossary.Service Health: Azure’s page for incidents and planned maintenance that affect your subscription’s regions and services.
glossary.Trusted Advisor: AWS’s free checks for cost, security, fault tolerance and limits. Basic support shows the security and limit checks.
glossary.support plan: The AWS support tier an account pays for: Basic (free), Developer, Business, Enterprise. It sets response times and which tools are unlocked.
glossary.CloudTrail: AWS’s audit log: every console click and API call, who made it and when. Event history keeps 90 days free.
glossary.Entra ID: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) — the identity service behind every Azure sign-in: users, groups, MFA, and the roles RBAC assigns.
glossary.security group (Entra): A group of users in Entra ID. Assign a role to the group once, and every member gets it.
glossary.user group: A group of IAM users in AWS. Attach a policy to the group once, and every member gets it.
glossary.MFA: Multi-factor authentication — a second proof at sign-in (an app code, a key), so a stolen password alone is not enough.
glossary.ADR: Architecture Decision Record — one page that says what was decided, what was rejected, and why, so the next team does not reopen it.

red.blurb: You’re the ethical attacker — you find and prove the weaknesses before a real attacker does.
red.arc: Wk1 recon → Wk2 scan for weaknesses → Wk3 exploit with proof → Wk4 write up findings.
red.handsOffTo: GRC (your findings) and Blue (your attack evidence)
red.waitsOnFrom: GRC (the signed scope that authorizes testing)

blue.blurb: You’re the defender — you harden the systems, watch for the attack, and respond when it happens.
blue.arc: Wk1 harden the hosts → Wk2 set up monitoring → Wk3 detect & contain the attack → Wk4 report the incident.
blue.handsOffTo: GRC (what you hardened and the incident write-up)
blue.waitsOnFrom: GRC (the hardening standard) and Red (the attack to detect)

grc.blurb: You’re governance — you set the rules, score the risk, and turn everyone’s work into the reports.
grc.arc: Wk1 scope & asset inventory → Wk2 risk register → Wk3 policy & response plan → Wk4 final report & briefing.
grc.handsOffTo: Red & Blue (scope, standards) and leadership (the final report)

redteam.blurb: AI Red Team — you test the Hub’s AI on your own instance and prove each case with evidence.
redteam.arc: Wk1 two cases → Wk2 six cases mapped → Wk3 automate the suite → Wk4 reproduce and four paper cases.
redteam.handsOffTo: the AI Defender (what to block and log)
redteam.waitsOnFrom: the Governance Lead (the signed lab rule)

defender.blurb: AI Defender — you build the controls, logging and alerts that stop and catch each case.
defender.arc: Wk1 close SA-1, log everything → Wk2 guardrails and redaction → Wk3 pipeline gates and alerts → Wk4 rebuild clean and hand over.
defender.handsOffTo: the Governance Lead (controls for the register)
defender.waitsOnFrom: the AI Red Team (the proven cases)

governance.blurb: AI Governance Lead — you map the system, own the risks and rules, and sign each release.
governance.arc: Wk1 map and sign v1 → Wk2 data and compliance → Wk3 shadow AI and accuracy → Wk4 accept risks and answer customers.
governance.waitsOnFrom: both teammates (cases and controls for the release)
